column2: Having worshipped him, the king then went into the water of the Narmada and worshipped Lakshmeshvara, standing there according to rule.
Then he went to Meghanada, and the sun set; while the king stood meditating on the one whose form is Time,
at that moment his fierce horse too became a sky-goer, bearing a divine body and surrounded by apsarases,
and in the aerial car of the king of the gods it went to Indra's city. The bitch that had been following the king on his pilgrimage
also took on a divine body and went to heaven in an aerial car. Seeing this, Dharmasena was filled with wonder
and said to the one in horse form, "What is this?", O Bharata. The sky-goer spoke: "Why do you grieve, O king?
Glories are won by austerity, by hardship borne in one's own body; go on foot, for you have travelled on another's feet.
Make the pilgrimage again, and then you will attain perfection." Then the king, having heard those words,
set out again on the second day to worship the lingas; having worshipped the five lingas, he came back to the Narmada.
When he saw Meghanada, he saw the god at the door: five-faced, ten-armed, three-eyed, trident in hand,
mounted on the bull, the womb of the world, with the moon as his crest. Seeing the lord of the god of gods, he praised the supreme Lord:
Victory, god Mahadeva, destroyer of great sins! I am sunk in the ocean of worldly existence; lift me out now.
Hara said: "Choose a boon, fortunate one, whatever is in your mind; I will give it without doubt, for you are Shiva's devotee, son."

If you are pleased with me, god, make me your companion; and whatever man worships the five lingas in a single day,
skandapuran:81:36	let him be your follower, god — this is my boon. Hearing Dharmasena's words, Hara said, "So be it,"
and taking the king he went to Kailasa; he made King Dharmasena abide in his own body, O king.
This I have told you, O king, an ancient history; by hearing and reciting it one gains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
He practised austerity for thousands of divine years, fortunate one; in his lovely hermitage sages of praised vows
dwelt, living on water and eating dry leaves; some there were without food, pondering the means of liberation.
Meanwhile, O king, two gandharvas, Shakra's singers named Heti and Praheti, went to Shakra's assembly.
There they saw a young woman, the best of the apsarases, Yudhishthira; at the very sight the two gandharvas were tormented by Love's arrows.
Heti with the cry of a cock and Praheti with that of a peacock, calling very sweetly, tried to win her over.
The slayer of Vritra, knowing their intention, laid a curse on them:
When a hundred divine years are complete you will come here again. So the two gandharvas entered animal births, Yudhishthira,
birds lovely to see, of evil conduct, remembering their former birth; crossing over all the holy places, they saw Narada.
The gandharvas said: "Brahma's son of good conduct, rich in austerity, tell us by what deed we two shall be released."
Narada said: "On the southern bank of the Narmada is the auspicious hermitage of Mrikanda, a holy place considered supreme for release from animal birth.
When you bathe in the water of the Narmada there, everything will come about." Then Heti and Praheti bathed well and took divine forms;
by a single bath the two birds attained divinity. Having bathed according to this rule and meditated on the god Sadashiva,
the two, reciting the Aghora mantra, remained ever in meditation, O king. Meanwhile, O king, there rose from Patala
an auspicious linga there, shining like a hundred suns, Yudhishthira — one Kukkuteshvara and the other Mayureshvara.
The two gandharvas, seated in an aerial car, went to Shakra's palace. A man who bathes at that holy place is not born again into existence.
By bathing and offering sesame water the ancestors reach the supreme goal. Whoever gives up his life there, helplessly or willingly,
has no return to the dreadful ocean of worldly existence. Worms, moths, birds and reptiles there,
frogs and even sinful trees, on dying go to Shiva's state.
The Siddhalinga Harinesha, and likewise Dhanurishvara; know also Baneshvara, and likewise Lubdhakeshvara.
Having worshipped these in linga form, one goes to Shiva. I shall tell you an ancient story, Yudhishthira.
A hunter named Arjuna, born of low caste, roaming in the hunt, O king, came to the bank of the Narmada.
Seeing a herd of deer he ran again and again; they all fled, but one deer remained behind.
That antelope was struck at midday on the bank of the Narmada; it fell lifeless and again bore a divine body,
and went to Brahma's world in an aerial car yoked with swans. When the deer had gone, the hunter was filled with thought:
I have committed many great sins again and again; what goal shall I go to? Death is best for me.
Having reflected thus, O king, he fell into the water of the Narmada; at that moment he gained a divine body and came to the city of the gandharvas.
When he had gone to the world of the gods, his bow and arrow remained in the water. These four lingas are famous in the three worlds:
Harineshvara, Banesha, Lubdhesha and Dhanurishvara; the fifth is Rameshvara — one should glorify the five lingas.
He has no return to the dreadful ocean of worldly existence. A man who bathes at that holy place, O king, goes to Shiva's city;
the killing of a brahmin and other sins dissolve, lord of the earth. One who dies there fasting, half in the water, attains Shiva.
The merit at Kanakhala, at the meeting of the Ganga and the ocean, at the confluence of the white and dark rivers, and especially at other holy places,
the merit at Arbuda and at the Amara mountain — the fruit a man obtains from all holy places headed by the Ganga,
he obtains that merit at this holy place, no doubt. With rule and mantra one should satisfy the ancestors and gods;
he rescues ten generations before and after. And a mortal, becoming pure and collected, should give a fee;
having performed the nyasa described before, he should offer the eightfold flower with the eight mantras taught in the scriptures, mentally; hear them too.
The flower of water, of Soma, of fire, of wind, of earth, of the trees, and seventh the flower of Prajapati,
and eighth the flower of Shiva; hear their explanation. The water flower is known as water; that of Soma is milk mixed with honey;
that of fire is incense and lamp; that of wind is sandal and the like; that of earth is bulbs, roots and so on; that of the trees consists of fruits;
that of Prajapati is food and the like; and the flower of Shiva is worship. Non-violence is the first flower, restraint of the senses a flower,
and third the flower of compassion; by these the gods are pleased. One should worship with austerity and devotion at this holy place, lord of men,
and give an umbrella, a chowrie, a bed and sandals; by that worship alone three generations are honoured,
and he dwells in the world of heaven until the deluge. Whoever with devotion has the trident-bearer bathed,
with the five nectars and with yakshakardama and saffron, and anoints the lord of the gods with sandal, aloe and the like —
the twice-born who worship with flowers of many kinds, who recite the Rudra, the Purusha Sukta and each his own Sutra,
the mantras beginning "ishe tva", the Jyotir Brahmana, the Gayatri, the Madhu and the Mandala Brahmana —
those persons who recite with devotion this japa arising from the Yajur Veda, the divine rite called Devavrata, went to his city.
Long ago, great king, there was an invincible one named Andhaka; he worshipped Shiva, attending on him for a long time.
The blessed god was pleased: "Ask a boon, you of good vows." Having obtained the boon, the daitya Andhaka ran off joyfully.
In the city people were seen with vessels filled with gems; with vessels of unbroken rice, a hundred thousand women of his,
brahmins reciting mantras with auspicious sounds, and all the citizens with ministers and servants, with the royal horses, chariots and elephants,
congratulated the king; living there joyful and thriving, he was not overcome by the gods.
Knowing that he had obtained the boon, the gods became alarmed; gathering together, they all went to Shakra for refuge.
Seeing the gods assembled, Shakra said: "Why have you all come, dwellers in heaven?
And how has fear arisen? Tell me, great gods."
The gods said: "In the mortal world there has arisen a sinful, arrogant one named Andhaka;
fallen into fear of him, we have come to you for refuge." Meanwhile the fierce danava, proud of his strength,
alone, mounted on a chariot and furnished with many weapons, Andhaka, tiger among kings, went to Shakra's city,
furnished with golden ramparts and adorned with many houses, always inaccessible to the host of enemies, best of kings.
The asura entered it with ease, as if it were his own house. Then Shakra rose and gave him his own seat.
Andhaka sat down there on Shakra's own lovely seat. Shakra said: "Why have you come here? What is your business? Tell me.
Whatever wealth is ours I will give you, danava." Andhaka said: "I do not desire wealth, nor elephants, nor horses.
Show me today your own adornment of heaven: the great elephant Airavata, the Sindhu horse Uchchaihshravas,
Urvashi and all the others, the three kinds of music, and your other glories, lord of Shachi."
Hearing these words of his, Shakra, overwhelmed with fear, showed Andhaka all these things.
Then, having come with the gods, yakshas, gandharvas and kinnaras, the apsarases danced there to many kinds of music, O king.
Seeing the apsarases then, his mind was bewildered, and by him all the hosts of gods were terrified, best of kings.
In battles of many kinds there, dreadful with discus, thunderbolt and other weapons, all the gods were tormented and many were destroyed.
The Adityas, the Maruts and the rest were routed on the field of battle; as beasts of prey attacked by a lion scatter in the forest,
so by that one alone all the gods were turned to flight. By force he oppressed the people in the lands and villages ceaselessly;
by intimidation milk, vegetables and clothing were seized; he did not respect their words, delighting in tormenting the people.
Seizing Shakra's wife, the danava went home. Then the gods and Shakra went to Brahma for refuge,
with elephants like mountains and horses like elephants, with chariots like the sky yoked with lions and tigers,
with tortoises, makaras, deer, rams and serpents; the gods headed by Indra reached Brahma's world.
Seeing the lotus-born god, they bowed to the lord and praised him: "Victory, god, lord of the world, victory, maker of creation!
Lotus-born, best of gods, we have come to you alone for refuge." Hearing the anxious words of the gods of cultivated self,
Brahma spoke to Vasava in a voice deep as a cloud: "Why have you come, gods, and why are you all pale?
By whom have you all been dishonoured? Tell me all of it." The gods said: "A danava named Andhaka, proud of his strength —
by him all the hosts of gods have been stripped of wealth and gems; having struck down the hosts of gods, lord, with axe, discus, sword and lance,
the danava seized Shakra's wife and went off by force." Hearing their words, Brahma, Grandsire of the world,
the blessed one, pondered the killing of that demon: "The sinful danava cannot be slain even by all the gods and asuras."
Then all the gods headed by Shakra praised Janardana: "Victory to you, god, lord of the gods, whose half-body is Lakshmi;
protect us quickly, lord of the gods, for we have come to you for refuge." Janardana said: "Welcome to you, fortunate ones; welcome to those who speak.
What is to be done? Tell me everything, the cause I wish to know; let him by whom you were humiliated go to Yama's abode."
Thus addressed, all the gods told him truly, and trembling, with faces downcast, they showed him their limbs:

Defeated by Andhaka, lord, we have been deprived of our kingdom.
skandapuran:84:62	Protect us, god, as a father his sons; slay the enemy here together with his sons and kin. Saying "So be it" to the lotus-seated one, the lord, whose footstool is saluted by gods and asuras...

You will find no peace here once looked upon by my gaze; you are no more able than a gayal before a tiger, Hari.
skandapuran:85:10	As a mouse that has come as prey before a cat, so you are not able, even standing before me.
Then, seeing the lord of the god of gods, bearing conch, discus and mace, four-armed, bright, offering him single combat,
seeing the mace-bearing god, he bowed on the ground with eight limbs. Andhaka said: "Victory, Krishna, for you are the Supreme; Vishnu, Jishnu, salutation again and again.
To Hrishikesha, to Kesha, to the sustainer of the world, to Achyuta; salutation to the lotus-naveled one, salutation to the one garlanded with lotuses,
to the god Janardana, wearer of yellow garments; salutation always to Govinda, and salutation to the one who lies on the ocean.
Salutation to the one of terrible mouth, to Narasimha the roarer; to the bearer of the Sharnga bow, of smiling face, bearing conch, discus and mace.
Salutation to the one in dwarf form, who strode across the three worlds; salutation to the one in boar form; to the one whose form is sacrifice, salutation to you.
Vasudeva, salutation to you; salutation to the destroyer of Kaitabha; son of Vasudeva and lord, salutation to you, leader of the gods.
Vishnu, lord of the god of gods, sustainer of the world, Prajapati — salutation again and again even to those who bow to you.
To the god of all beings, the wise Vasudeva, to him the sacrificial Boar, to Vishnu of boundless radiance,
to the ordainer of the gunas, salutation to you again and again." The god said: "I am pleased, lord of the danavas; choose a boon as you wish.
I give you a boon today, since you now ask." Andhaka said: "If you are pleased with me, god, and wish to give me a boon here,
then give me, god, a supremely splendid battle." The Blessed Lord said: "How can I give you battle when I have been pleased by you?
I can feel no anger toward you, so how shall I fight, Andhaka? If your mind is set on battle, without doubt,
then go quickly to the god Maheshvara." Andhaka said: "By the grace of that god I am victorious in the three worlds;
how could I wage battle with that Shankara? Tell us." Hearing this from the danava, the Blessed One said this:
I shall tell you how he will fight with you: go to the peak of Kailasa and shake it again and again.
When that mountain was shaken, the three worlds trembled; its peaks fell, shattering in many pieces;
the four oceans, O king, became one on every side. Rudra, with Uma, his mind absorbed in pleasure,
Shankara, trembling, fell together with Parvati. Clasping the lord of the gods tightly, Uma said:

Why does the mountain tremble, and why does the earth quake? The seven netherworlds and the seven heavens shake.
skandapuran:85:31	Is it the end of the age, god? You should tell me. Maheshvara said: "Whose evil thought is this — even one of my attendants?
If this is shattered on his forehead, he shall go to Yama's abode. I was resting in meditation on Kailasa, and I have been roused from sleep.
I shall slay him, no doubt, even if he were Shanmukha." Then he reflected, "It is Andhaka, who knows me,"
and he considered a means by which he could be slain in a moment. Then the gods assembled, headed by Indra and Brahma,
and made a chariot consisting of the gods, furnished with every mark; some gods stood on the wheels, some on the tip of the pole,
some on the axle, O king, some on the yoke and reins, and some on the chariot's pillar, the top of the banner and elsewhere.
Having made it thus of the gods, the lord of the world mounted it, and Maheshvara in wrath went out to where the danava was.
He harassed the danavas and filled the sky like the sun with his shafts; neither the sun nor the quarters nor the moon could be seen there.
Then the king of the danavas fitted the fire weapon; the whole circle of the gods was burned there by the arrows,
and, burning with the arrows, they came to the god for refuge. Then the god of gods released the Varuna weapon,
and by that Varuna weapon the fire weapon was quenched. Then the danava released the wind weapon, best of kings,
and the god too, filled with wrath, released the serpent weapon; the wind was devoured by the enraged serpents, no doubt.
Then the mighty danava released the Garuda weapon; by it the serpent weapon was torn into a hundred pieces and was seen no more.
Then the god of gods released the Narasimha weapon; warding off weapons with weapons, the two fought each other.
The battle was even, dear one, terrifying to gods and asuras, with discus, arrows, iron shafts, lances, swords and hammers,
with calf-tooth arrows, bhallas and fine karnikara arrows; thus he could not be slain by the danavas' many weapons.
Then, with terrible tusks, swords, iron shafts and lances — as a bride goes with face lowered in shame on seeing her mothers-in-law,
as a praiseworthy Gauda bride does not touch another's limbs, so the weapons did not touch their bodies. Then, casting aside their weapons, they came to wrestling,
seizing hands with hands and striking with fists; with holds, blows of the hand and the like they fought each other.
The danava crushed the god in the hollow of his arm, and then the god Maheshvara lay motionless and fainted.
Knowing him to have fainted, the danava thought: "Alas, alas, what a grievous thing has been done today by me, a wicked sinner!
What am I to do here now, and how shall I go?" Then, taking the lord of the gods, he went to Mount Kailasa,
and laying him down as he lay unconscious, Andhaka went away in a moment. Then the god of gods Maheshvara regained consciousness,
and as soon as he saw himself lying in his own abode he thought: "I have been humiliated by that wicked one."
Seized by a surge of wrath he went out toward the danava; holding an iron club weighing a thousand bharas,
the lord saw the danava and hurled it at his head; the danava, laughing in the battle, struck back with his sword.
The lord of the god of gods took the excellent arrow of Kubera and at that moment struck him in the heart with the blazing shaft.
Then the danava there, vomiting streams of blood, was turned face downward and pierced through by the trident.
Pierced on the point of the trident, the sinner spun like a wheel; and from the drops of blood from his body that fell on the ground
sinful danavas arose, weapons in hand. Then the god was harassed by the danavas again and again.
The god then called to mind Durga, the terrible Chamunda; the terrible goddess came, furnished with ten thousand weapons,
great-tusked, great-bodied, tawny-eyed, with long ears. The goddess said to the lord of gods: "Command me, Maheshvara."
The god said: "Drink the danava's blood as you please, good lady, and carefully take up what has fallen on the earth, Durga;
you should help today in the slaying of the danava." Then all those danavas were slain by the sword in thousands.
Andhaka too, seeing those danavas gone to death, then praising the god Maheshvara with well-nourished words —
the mighty one had cried, "Stand, stand!" to the lord of gods and to Chandi; from the hole pierced by the trident he poured out much blood
and filled the earth girdled by the four oceans. Standing in the sky and fixed on the trident's point,
held on the god's shoulder and raining streams of blood, he filled the earth with its mountains, woods and forests.
Though checked, the blood rose to Maheshvara's waist, and then it came up to the god's chest.
Then the gods were distressed and fled in all directions. He then rubbed eight limbs of his own body,
and eight beings of Bhairava form arose from Maheshvara, all with terrible tusks, crying out loudly,
all with skull-cups in their hands, bearing swords and knives. "Drink all the blood," said the supreme Lord.
The blood was drunk by them, the blood was exhausted and the ground stood dry; his body was dried up, leaving only bone and skin.
And the danava Andhaka, moving in the sky, spoke. Andhaka said: "Victory, god, lord of the world, bearing half your body as Uma,
mounted on the bull seat, with the moon as your crest; victory to the one with the khatvanga in hand, who bears the Ganga on his head;
to the crusher of Smara here, to the Lord, salutation to you; to the destroyer of Pushan's teeth, lord of the ganas, salutation again and again.
Victory to the one of beautiful body, to the formless, salutation again and again; to the destroyer of Brahma's head, lord of the universe, eternal,
to the one ever dwelling in the cremation ground, ever of Bhairava form. You are all-pervading, you are the maker, you are the destroyer and no other.
You are the earth, you are the directions, you are light and radiance; you are the wind of all beings, Maheshvara in the form of living creatures.
You are Soma, you are Budha, you are Guru and Bhargava; you are the son of the Sun, lord of the god of gods, and likewise the son of the earth.
The stars that are seen in the sky, the moon and the sun — all these exist by your grace, Maheshvara."
Having thus praised the god of gods in many ways, the danava bowed to Maheshvara with joined hands.
Shankara said: "Well done, well done, great being; ask a boon, danava. I am the giver and you the asker; I give you whatever you wish."
Andhaka said: "If you are pleased, lord of gods, if a boon is to be given me, then I must be placed near you and nowhere else,
ash-smeared, matted-haired, bearing the trident, three-eyed and four-armed, with a tiger skin as upper garment and a serpent as sacred thread —
all this I desire, if you will give it, Shankara." While he spoke from the trident's point, Maheshvara was pleased.
The Lord said: "I give you today the boon you have spoken of; as I declared to you before, you shall be Bhringiriti."
The god said: "Welcome to you, fortunate ones, all of you who have come here; the danava has been slain there for your sake, no doubt.
But because of his blood my trident is not seen clean; what am I to do now? Tell me, Grandsire.
He whom I slew was your descendant, brahmin; I wish to make a proper pilgrimage to the holy places, no doubt.
Rise, and let all of you who have come here go." Then with all the gods he set out for Prabhasa.
Though he bathed in all the holy places from Prabhasa to the meeting of the Ganga and the ocean, the trident did not become clean.
As a cloth dyed with indigo does not become white, so the darkened trident did not become clean.
Then the god, accompanied by the gods, went to the Narmada and carefully bathed at its northern and southern banks.
Going to the southern bank, to the mountain called Bhrigu, Mahadeva stayed there with the gods, lord of the earth.
That place was delightful to all the dwellers in heaven; knowing it to be a special holy place, the god Maheshvara stayed there.
He split the mountain with his trident, and by it Rasatala was split; the trident became clean, and no stain was seen anywhere.
From Patala came forth the Ganga named Bhogavati, and a holy place arose there, renowned as Shulabheda.
When the sun is seized by Rahu, the most holy Sarasvati is there; there is a second confluence, like the Veni of the white and dark rivers.
There is the god Brahma himself, the excellent linga Brahmesha, on whose southern side is the god Janardana himself;
Vishnu himself is present there, established on the seats. The line drawn by the trident there became a water-bearing channel, O king,
and that water went to where the water of the river Reva is; there is a most holy linga, renowned as Chakratirtha.
The lord of the gods, having bathed according to rule at Shulabheda, considered himself pure, with no stain at all on his body.
And on its northern side, reaching the god of gods, the world's guru, the trident-bearer, he worshipped him with care.
This holy place contains all holy places and is supreme above all holy places, holier than all holy things, excellent, destroying all sorrow.
Having established the holy place there, the god of gods, world's guru, set guards there and installed Vinayaka there;
a hundred and eight kshetrapalas guard the holy place carefully; they create obstacles for anyone who wishes to stay there:
some are given worry about their families, some worry about their farms, some take service, intent on earning money;
others speak ill behind people's backs, others delight in violence, others pursue others' wives, others brood on wealth;
others too say thus: "How can one go to holy places? My wife and children are tormented by hunger."
From men of sinful conduct fallen into the net of delusion, the god's ganas guard that auspicious holy place.
Holy people who are steadfast obtain their bath there, in the Payoshni, the divine river and especially the Bhogavati.
This confluence is holy like the Veni of the white and dark rivers. Seeing the holy place, all the gods, delighted in mind,
being in the god's presence, described it to one another: "They know this holy place, lord of gods, to be equal to Gaya.
A holy place more secret than the secret has not been and will not be." Having worshipped the trident-bearer, Brahma and the others with the gods,
the ganas, the gandharvas, Yama, Varuna and Vasava, and all the gods and asuras, with dance, song and hymns —
where the god struck with the point of his trident, best of kings, three pits arose, full of water, lord of men,
whirling, best of men, marked with the great thunderbolt, destroying all sins and removing all sorrows.
A man who bathes at that holy place devoted to fasting, even without initiation and mantra, is freed from the bondage of existence.
Whoever again bathes according to rule with the five mantras — the five mantras taught in the Veda — and with pots containing gold,
with the ten-syllabled and the three five-syllabled mantras, separately for the twice-born, the holy place is praised, lord of men;
whether brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya, shudra or woman, meditating on the three gods, O king, and bathing according to rule,
the man who drinks the water with the ten-syllabled mantra — as when drunk at Kedara, so in the pool, no doubt.
Furnished with five ra-sounds, adorned with the syllable ksha, joined with two Oms — this is the recitation here.
Whoever bathes there according to rule, with senses controlled, and satisfies the ancestors and gods with water mixed with sesame,
rescues twenty generations of his family, ten before and ten after. Whoever performs shraddha on the Ganga and at Panchatirtha
obtains that fruit there at Shulabheda, no doubt. Whoever, following the rule, gives a gift there with devotion,
the fruit of what he has done there, or of his good deed, is imperishable. As there is merit at the field of Gaya in all rites,
so there is merit at Shulabheda through bathing, giving and offerings. Whoever gives there with devotion gold, a cow, land or water,
food grown from the field, a bed, clothes and ornaments, a house filled all round with food and wealth,
a pair of yoked animals, a fine new plough and two draught oxen — whoever gives these gifts to a brahmin versed in the Veda,
knowing him to be learned in the Veda, of good family, pure and with senses controlled — there is no end to his gift.
Even one gift in the thirteen days becomes thirteenfold.
At shraddha, in the daily sacrifice and especially in giving — tell me this, god: to whom should a gift not be given?
The Lord said: "As an elephant made of wood, as a deer made of leather, so is a brahmin without learning; the three bear only the name.
The sick, one with missing or extra limbs, the one-eyed, the son of a remarried woman, one who has broken his vow, the kunda and golaka — these are not pure for shraddha or gifts.
The Mahishya, the Vrishala, the thief and especially the usurer — such brahmins are always to be avoided; afterwards one praises the honour.
A twice-born man who accepts gifts without knowledge of the proper time — no gift should be given to him; it becomes useless and fruitless.
Give to the poor, O king, never to the prosperous; medicine is wholesome for the sick — what use is medicine to the healthy?"
Uttanapada said: "What is the rule, god, and how is the rite of shraddha performed? And by whom is a gift to be given? You should tell me this."
The god said: "Having performed shraddha at home with devotion, well bathed, with senses controlled, restraining speech, one should offer libations without exceeding the number.
Then going to Shulabheda and bathing according to rule, whoever performs shraddha at the five places with offerings to gods and ancestors,
and offers pindas with milk-rice, honey and ghee, obtains that fruit at that holy place, no doubt.
Whoever gives sandals, especially to brahmins, goes mounted on an aerial car, surrounded by immortals.
Whoever gives a fine house filled with the seven grains dwells in the world of heaven in the finest golden mansion.
Whoever gives a sesame cow with its calf according to rule dwells on the vault of heaven until the deluge.
At home or in the forest, at a holy place or on bad roads, whoever gives water and food does not see Yama's world.
Imperishable is the gift of food, and likewise of water and land; there has been and will be no gift higher than the gift of food."
Uttanapada said: "How is the gift of a daughter to be made, god? Tell me that — the acceptance, the gratification, the marriage of a daughter and its provisions.
To whom should a gift be given so that it becomes imperishable — the best, the middling or in some way the least,
of rajas, of tamas, or leading to the highest good?" The Lord said: "Of all gifts, the gift of a daughter is pre-eminent.
Whoever with supreme devotion, approaching carefully, gives to one of good family, of good form and especially one who knows virtue,
at an auspicious lagna and muhurta, a daughter adorned, and gives horses, elephants and garments with devotion,
his dwelling will be in the state free from sickness. He by whom a daughter, dearer even than life, has been given,
has given all this, the three worlds with moving and unmoving. The evil-minded man who arranges to take wealth for his daughter
becomes a chandala by deed and on death becomes a silkworm. Whoever asks for money for a daughter, whether rich or poor,
becomes one whose food is not to be eaten, excluded from all things; and whoever, greedy of tongue, eats in his house, O king,
is purified by the chandrayana or the taptakrichchhra." The king said: "One who has no wealth, when the time for a daughter's marriage comes —
how should he perform the marriage? Tell me this, lord." The god said: "The daughter's marriage should be carried out with one's own wealth;
but if one names the daughter when asking, there is no fault in the asker. A gift made by approaching the recipient is the best, one made on invitation is middling,
one made when asked is the lowest, and a gift for service is fruitless. Nor should the gift of a daughter be given to one who is incapable.
A capable learned man carries across, as a log thrown into water floats; as a boat does, so the learned man carries one to the further shore.
One who, having established the sacred fires, accepts gifts from a shudra becomes a shudra in this birth and on death is born a dog.
The labours of a brahmin who keeps the agnihotra become vain if, without distress, the twice-born accepts an improper gift;
it destroys all his merit, like a broken boat in the water; what was earned with great toil it destroys in a moment.
Thus merit earned with pain goes to the shudra and nowhere else. A gift made to gain a lakh by courtesy is an offence;
what is given to vessels of fame becomes useless, lord of the earth."
Shankara said: "As merit for the sake of one's father is excellent at all times, so this holy place is holy for bathing, giving and offerings.
Especially they perform shraddha on the first days of the four yugas; and hear, dear one, the fourteen first days of the manvantaras:
the bright ninth of Ashvina, the twelfth of Kartika, the third in the month of Chaitra and likewise of Bhadrapada,
the tenth of Ashadha, the seventh of Magha, the dark eighth of Shravana and the full moon of Ashadha,
the new moon of Phalguna, the auspicious eleventh of Pausha, and the bright fifteenths of Kartika, Phalguna, Chaitra and Jyeshtha.
These first days of the manvantaras are declared to give endless fruit; so too the northern and southern solstices,
the full moons of Kartika, Magha and Vaishakha, the third, the full moon of Chaitra, the sixth and likewise that of Proshthapada —
these are all times for shraddha, and what is given becomes imperishable. Having fasted on the eleventh of the bright fortnight in the month of Madhu,
one should keep vigil through the night near Vishnu's footprint, and give gifts according to one's means — gold, cows and garments.
Whoever worships Vishnu with incense, lamp and food offering, garlands, flowers and sandal, and tells his story in Puranic recitation,
the twice-born who recites the hymns of the Rik, Yajus, Saman and Atharvan, is freed from all sins and goes to Vishnu's world.
Whoever performs shraddha at dawn, carefully feeding brahmins, and gives gifts according to his means — gold, cows and garments —
his ancestors are satisfied until the deluge, and the giver of shraddha dwells where the god Janardana is.
Then on the thirteenth one should go to where the one called Guhavasi stands; seeing Markandeshvara, the Lord, one is freed from all sins."
Uttanapada said: "The supremely splendid linga in the middle of the cave, god — you should tell me by whom the god was installed."
The Lord said: "It is famous in the three worlds under the name Markandeshvara. The best of the twice-born who recites the Brihat and Rathantara of the Sama Veda,
the Atharvashiras of the Atharvan, the Vrishakapi hymn and the Shivasankalpa, is freed from all sins
and goes to the supreme place where the god Maheshvara is. Those who with devotion wash his feet
obtain the merit of the gift of a cow, no doubt. One should feed brahmins there with milk-rice, honey and ghee;
by feeding even one, a thousand are fed. One should give gold, silver and cloth with devotion to the twice-born;
by that the gods, men and ancestors are satisfied. Men who bathe with devotion at an eclipse of the moon or the sun,
whoever worships the gods and especially performs japa and oblation, and gives gifts according to his means to a brahmin versed in the Veda —
a jewel of a horse, a jewel of an elephant and the tulapurusha; whoever gives there a cart filled with the seven grains,
and a plough yoked with two young draught oxen — cows, land, sesame and gold, the desired gift, should be given to a worthy recipient.
A wise man desiring good should give nothing to an unworthy one. Since the earth itself upholds all beings,
it should be given to a brahmin, rich with all crops. Hear too, king of kings, the fruit of the gift of a cow:
as long as the calf's two feet and mouth are seen in the womb, until she releases the calf, the cow is to be known as the earth itself.
Whoever by some means or other presents her to a brahmin has given the earth with its mountains, woods and forests;
given thus, she rescues twenty-one generations. A cow with silver hooves, a bronze milking pail, with her calf and giving milk,
holy people give when the moon is seized by Rahu. For every other gift there is a measure, lord of men,
but at an eclipse of the moon or the sun there is no measure of the gift. Where cows are seen, all the holy places are there;
one should know sacrifice to be there; there is no need for deliberation. A man who, remembering that holy place again, goes there,
or who hears of it, becomes a follower of Rudra."
Renowned like Indraprastha, furnished with herds of white cows, crowded with many brahmins, resounding with the sound of the Vedas,
adorned with merchants of many kinds engaged in buying and selling, with towers, gateways and festivals,
beautified with divine temples and gardens, adorned with groves of plantains and lovely flowers and fruits of many kinds.
On its northern side is an excellent and auspicious garden, renowned in the three worlds as the Samandara forest,
covered with many trees and creepers, beautified with many flowers and filled with many mandara trees; hence it is called the Mandaraka forest.
